Endor
EN-dor
proper noun (place)
Hebrew 'En-dor (H5874), "spring/fountain of Dor," from 'ayin ("spring") + Dor. A town in the territory of Manasseh; famous for the medium ("witch") Saul consulted on the eve of his death.

Biblical Definition

Endor was a town in northern Israel famous as the home of the medium — the "witch of Endor" — whom King Saul consulted on the night before his death, in one of the most solemn and frightening episodes of the Old Testament. Saul, abandoned by God because of his disobedience, faced the Philistine army at Gilboa and was filled with dread. He had himself earlier "put away those that had familiar spirits, and the wizards, out of the land" (1 Sam 28:3), in obedience to the Law that forbade consulting the dead and condemned mediums and necromancers (Lev 19:31; 20:6, 27; Deut 18:10-12). But now, when "the LORD answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets" (1 Sam 28:6), Saul in desperation disguised himself and went by night to the medium at Endor, asking her to bring up the spirit of the dead Samuel. What happened next is debated, but the text presents it as a genuine and terrifying appearance: Samuel appeared (the medium herself cried out in fear, suggesting this was not her usual trickery), and pronounced God's final word of doom upon Saul — that the kingdom was torn from him, that Israel would be delivered to the Philistines, and that "to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me" (1 Sam 28:19). The next day Saul and his sons died at Gilboa. The Chronicler gives the divine verdict on the whole affair: "So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD... and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; And enquired not of the LORD: therefore he slew him" (1 Chr 10:13-14). Endor stands as a dark and permanent warning against the sin of consulting the dead and the occult — a sin God expressly forbids and severely judges. It is the desperate resort of a man who, having refused to seek God while he could, turns at last to the forbidden powers of darkness; and it sealed his doom. The believer is to seek the LORD, who answers those who come to Him in faith, and to abhor every form of occult divination as rebellion against God.

Webster 1828 Definition

A town in northern Israel, home of the medium ("witch of Endor") whom Saul consulted the night before his death, when the LORD would no longer answer him (1 Sam 28); Samuel appeared and pronounced doom; Saul died for, among other sins, seeking a medium rather than the LORD (1 Chr 10:13-14).

ENDOR, proper noun. Hebrew 'En-dor (H5874), "spring of Dor"; a town in northern Israel (Manasseh).

Home of the medium ("witch of Endor") whom Saul consulted the night before the battle of Gilboa (1 Sam 28).

Saul had earlier banished mediums per the Law (1 Sam 28:3; cf. Lev 19:31; Deut 18:10-12), but turned to one in desperation when God would not answer him.

Samuel appeared and pronounced God's final doom: "to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me" (1 Sam 28:19).

The Chronicler's verdict: Saul died for his transgression and for consulting a medium rather than the LORD (1 Chr 10:13-14).

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 28:6-7 — "And when Saul enquired of the LORD, the LORD answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets. Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her."

Deuteronomy 18:10-12 — "There shall not be found among you any one that... useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch... or a necromancer. For all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD."

1 Samuel 28:19 — "Moreover the LORD will deliver Israel also with thee into the hand of the Philistines: and to morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me."

1 Chronicles 10:13-14 — "So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD... and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; And enquired not of the LORD: therefore he slew him."

Modern Corruption

Endor is corrupted when the episode is treated as harmless folklore or entertainment, when the divine prohibition of occult consultation is dismissed, or when Saul's sin is minimized rather than named as the rebellion that sealed his doom.

expand to see more

Occult-as-harmless misreading. The witch of Endor has passed into folklore and popular culture as a quaint or thrilling tale, and the wider world treats divination, mediumship, astrology, and contacting the dead as harmless entertainment or spiritual curiosity. Scripture treats them as abomination: "there shall not be found among you any one that... useth divination... or a necromancer. For all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD" (Deut 18:10-12). The Endor episode is no harmless ghost story; it is the account of a man's final, fatal sin — turning to the forbidden powers of darkness when he would no longer seek God. The occult is not neutral; it is rebellion against the LORD, and He forbids it under the severest terms.

Endor has no significant postmodern redefinition that softens its warning. The principal point worth recovering is the divine verdict on Saul: he died not only for his earlier disobedience but specifically "for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; And enquired not of the LORD" (1 Chr 10:13-14). The tragedy is double: Saul had refused to seek God in obedience while he could, and when God would no longer answer him, he turned at last to the very occult powers he had once banished. The lesson is searching and permanent: seek the LORD while He may be found (Isa 55:6); do not, having neglected Him, turn in the day of trouble to the forbidden powers of darkness, which can only seal the doom that disobedience has prepared.
